question: What does Zechariah see in the night vision among the myrtle trees, and what report do the riders bring about the earth?
The verb שׁוּב (shuv, “return”) opens the book: “return to Me... and I will return to you.” What does this reciprocity say about the relationship between God and the people?
Why does the angel ask “how long” after seventy years, and what words of comfort does God answer with?
The prophet recalls the fathers who did not listen: what lesson from the history of your family or community do you not want to repeat?
Why does the man with the measuring line go to Jerusalem, and why will the city have no walls?
The word חוֹמָה (chomah, “wall”) appears in a surprising image: what does it mean for the LORD to be “a wall of fire” around the city?
What new thing appears in verse 11 about the nations, and how does it relate to God's promise to dwell in the midst of Zion?
“Whoever touches you touches the apple of His eye”: how can this image of care change the way you see yourself before God?
Who is in the scene before the angel of the LORD, how is Joshua dressed, and what happens to his clothes?
The word שָׂטָן (satan, “accuser, adversary”) defines the role of the one standing at Joshua's right hand: what does this word reveal about the courtroom scene?
Who might the servant called “the Branch” be, and how do different readings, Jewish and Christian, understand this title?
Joshua is called “a burning stick snatched from the fire” and receives new clothes: what guilt or accusation do you need to hear God rebuke?
What is the lampstand the prophet sees like, and what stands beside it?
The word רוּחַ (ruach, “spirit, wind, breath”) is at the center of verse 6: what contrast does it make with “might” and “power”?
Why did some despise “the day of small things” in the rebuilding of the temple, and how does God respond to this?
What small beginning in your life have you been treating with contempt and may need to see differently?
What is written on the flying scroll, and against which houses does it go?
What does it mean that the woman called Wickedness is shut in a basket and carried to Shinar, far from the land?
The word רִשְׁעָה (rish‘ah, “wickedness”) names the woman in the basket: why does evil appear here as something that must be removed from the land, and not only punished?
Theft and false oaths “enter the house”: at what moments can dishonesty seem small yet affect your whole household?
How many chariots appear, what colors are their horses, and where do they go?
The word צֶמַח (tsemach, “Branch, sprout”) returns in this chapter: what roles does verse 13 assign to this man, and what is strange in their union?
Why are the crowns made with silver and gold brought by those who returned from captivity, and why are they placed on the head of a priest?
The promise ends with a condition: “if you diligently obey the voice of the LORD.” What part of your hope depends on your obedience?
What question do the men of Bethel bring to the priests and prophets?
The verb צוּם (tsum, “fast”) appears in God's answer: what does the question “was it really for Me that you fasted?” call into doubt?
Why, instead of answering about fasting, does God speak of true justice, mercy and care for the widow and the orphan?
The text speaks of hearts “as hard as flint”: what signs show that someone is stopping their ears to what God asks?
What will life in Jerusalem be like according to verses 4 and 5, and who will be in the squares?
The word אֶמֶת (emet, “truth”) is repeated in the chapter, even in the name of the city: what does it mean for a city to be called “the City of Truth”?
What happens to the fasts of mourning mentioned in chapter 7, and why is this change significant?
What scene does the chapter imagine with the ten men who grasp the robe of a Jew, and what does it reveal about the place of the nations?
Speaking the truth to your neighbor and not plotting evil against him: in which of your relationships is this proving hardest?
What neighboring cities and peoples are mentioned, and what is said about what remains of the Philistines in verse 7?
The king of verse 9 is called עָנִי (ani, “humble, poor”) and comes riding on a donkey's colt: what kind of king does this description present?
The Gospels link verse 9 to Jesus' entry into Jerusalem: what does verse 10 add about the peace this king brings?
The “prisoners of hope” are invited to return to the stronghold: what keeps your hope standing when you feel trapped?
Why did the people wander “like sheep,” according to verse 2, and of whom should they ask for rain?
The verb שָׁרַק (sharaq, “whistle”) describes how God will gather His people: what does this shepherd's image suggest about the return of the scattered?
What contrast does the chapter draw between the shepherds against whom God is angry and the LORD's own care for Judah and Joseph?
God says “they will be as though I had never rejected them”: how do you receive the idea of being completely restored?
What names does the prophet give the two staffs, and what happens to each of them?
What do the thirty pieces of silver as the shepherd's wages mean, and why does Matthew 27:9-10 recall this scene?
The verb רָעָה (ra‘ah, “shepherd”) runs through the chapter: what difference does the text show between the good shepherd and the “worthless shepherd”?
The foolish shepherd does not seek the lost or heal the injured: what responsibility of care do you have that you may be neglecting?
What images are used for Jerusalem before the peoples, such as the cup and the heavy stone?
The verb דָּקַר (daqar, “pierce”) appears in verse 10: who looks on the one who was pierced, and how does John 19:37 reread this phrase?
Why is the mourning described family by family, men and women apart, and what does this say about repentance?
The “Spirit of grace and prayer” leads to weeping: what place does sincere repentance have in your life of faith?
What will happen to the idols and the false prophets, and how will the latter come to present themselves?
The word מָקוֹר (maqor, “fountain”) opens the chapter: against what is this fountain opened, and for whom?
Why is the sword called against the shepherd, and what use does Jesus make of this verse in Mark 14:27?
God speaks of refining like silver and testing like gold: how have you been living through the trials that seem to refine your faith?
What happens to Jerusalem at the beginning of the chapter, and where will the LORD's feet stand on that day?
The word אֶחָד (echad, “one”) is repeated in verse 9: how does it echo the Shema of Deuteronomy 6:4, “the LORD is one”?
Why does the Feast of Tabernacles gain such prominence at the end of the book, and what does it mean that even the pots will be “holy to the LORD”?
If even the bells of the horses would bear “HOLY TO THE LORD,” what ordinary thing of your daily life could you live as something holy?
